title: Tuning the catalytic selectivity in electrochemical CO2 reduction on copper oxide-derived nanomaterials
abstract: Electrochemical conversion of CO2 to hydrocarbons can relieve both environmental and energy stresses. However, electrocatalysts for this reaction usually suffer from a poor product selectivity and a large overpotential. Here we report that tunable catalytic selectivity for hydrocarbon formation could be achieved on Cu nanomaterials with different morphologies. By tuning the electrochemical parameters, either Cu oxide nanowires or nanoneedles were fabricated and then electrochemically reduced to the corresponding Cu nanomaterials. The Cu nanowires preferred the formation of C2H4, while the Cu nanoneedles favored the production of more CH4, rather than C2H4. Our work provides a facile synthetic strategy for preparing Cu-based nanomaterials to achieve selective CO2 reduction.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
In the past few decades a significant increase in CO2 emission has occurred due to the combustion of fossil fuels [1]. As a low-cost and widely available carbon resource, CO2 could be recycled and reused to synthesize chemical commodities, which would alleviate both environmental and energy stresses [2–4]. Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to chemicals has attracted increasing interests, as it offers a mild, controllable and environmentally friendly way to convert CO2 into hydrocarbons with a reasonable conversion efficiency [5–7]. However, to enable this process, one of the most key technological challenges is the preparation of efficient and selective electrocatalysts [8,9]. Various metals have been exploited in previous
studies, as summarized in several review papers [10,11], and Cu has been demonstrated to be the only one that could catalyze CO2 to hydrocarbons at acceptable levels of efficiency. However, the widely explored polycrystalline Cu suffers poor selectivity and stability [12,13]. Therefore, numerous efforts have been made to improve the performance of Cu electrocatalysts. Hori and his coworkers [14,15] investigated the product selectivity between CH4 and C2H4, and reported that such a selectivity critically depended on the crystal orientation of Cu surface. This observation was further confirmed by other researchers. Koper et al. [16] found that the overpotentials of CO reduction to CH4 and C2H4 shifted, depending on the crystal orientation of Cu. Durand et al. [17] used computational methods to demonstrate that the nanostructure of Cu surface affected the selectivity in CO2 reduction. Schouten et al. [18], also applied theoretical calculations to validate that CH4 formation was favored on Cu(111), whereas C2H4 production was preferred on Cu(100) with a lower overpotential compared with CH4. Inspired by these works, various Cu electrode modification methods, such as electrodeposit [19,20], alloy [21] and ligand-stabilization [22], have been tried. It was reported that Cu2O nanofilms formed by air annealing of Cu exhibited an excellent activity and stability for CO production, and considerably lowered the overpotential [23]. Goncalves et al. [24] found that Cu electrodes with Cu electrodeposits preferred the formation of C2H4 and C2H6, rather than CH4 and CO, while H2 was still the dominated product. Whereas these treatments improved the reaction selectivity, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), which is considered as a side reaction, also increased. Furthermore, to fully control catalyst morphology toward selective CO2 reduction, more effective approaches are highly desired. Therefore, the main objective of this study was to prepare Cu oxide catalysts with appropriate nanostructure and morphology for selective CO2 reduction to form hydrocarbon. Through controlling the electrochemical Received April 6, 2014; accepted May 25, 2014 E-mail: hqyu@ustc.edu.cn
oxidation parameters, Cu oxide nanowires (NWs) and nanoneedles (NNs) could be synthesized on Cu foils, and their structures morphologies and electrocatalytic characteristics were examined. With these synthesized Cu oxide materials, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to hydrocarbons was explored. In this way, appropriate Cu-based nanomaterials for selective CO2 reduction were obtained.

sections.heading: 2 Materials and methods
sections.text:
2.1 Preparation and characterization of Cu oxide NWs and NNs
20 mm 20 mm Cu foils (Alfa Aesar Co., USA, 0.127 mm thickness, annealed, 99.9%) were ultrasonicallytreated in acetone, ethanol and 2 mol$L–1 HCl (Sinopharm Co., China, 36% – 38%) for 15 min, respectively. The treated Cu foils were then rinsed with deionized water, and transferred into a solution containing 200 g$L–1 of NaCl (Sinopharm Co., China, 99.99%) and 4 g$L–1 of NaOH (Sinopharm Co., China, 99.99%) in a 30°C water bath to prepare Cu oxide. The as-cleaned Cu foils were used as the working electrodes. A Pt wire was used as the counter electrode, and a KCl saturated Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode. Two electrochemical methods, potentiostatic and galvanostatic oxidations, were used to synthesize the Cu oxide nanomaterials. In the potentiostatic oxidation, a potential of – 0.1 V was applied to the Cu foil with a geometric area of 8 cm2 for 1800 s, leading to the formation of the Cu oxide NNs. While in the galvanostatic oxidation, an anodic current density of 0.5 mA$cm–2 was applied to the Cu foil for 1800 s, resulting in the formation of the Cu oxide NWs. The prepared Cu oxide electrodes were carefully rinsed with deionized water three times and dried under N2 atmosphere. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging was performed on a Sirion 200 SEM (FEI Co., USA). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis and auger electron spectroscopy (AES) were conducted using an ESCALAB 250 instrument (Thermo-VG Scientific Inc., USA) with a monochromatic Al Kα X-ray source.
2.2 Electrochemical CO2 reduction
The electrochemical CO2 reduction tests were conducted with a potentiostat (CHI 760D, CH Instrument Co., China) in a customized two-compartment cell separated by a proton exchange membrane (Nafion 212, Dupont Inc., USA). The catholyte contained 85 mL of 0.1 mol$L–1 KHCO3 (Sinopharm Co., China, 99.99%) saturated with CO2 at pH 6.8. The headspace volume of the cathodic compartment was 26 mL. A modified Cu electrode with a geometric surface area of 10 10 mm2 was used as the working electrode. A KCl saturated Ag/AgCl electrode
with a Luggin capillary was used as the reference electrode, and a Pt foil with the area of 20 mm 20 mm was used as the counter electrode. All the potential values presented in this paper were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) scale with the equation E (vs RHE) = E (vs Ag/AgCl)+ 0.210 V+ 0.0591 V pH [23]. To remove dissolved O2 in the electrolyte, continuous CO2 purging was applied for 30 min prior the experiments. The Cu oxide nanomaterials were pre-reduced before catalysis at – 1.0 V in 0.1 mol$L–1 KHCO3 saturated with CO2. The electrolysis time of each applied cathode potential was 12 min. The gaseous products were sampled at the 10th min and analyzed by gas chromatography (GC). H2 concentration was detected using an SP-6890 GC (Rainbow Instrument Co., China) equipped with a Molecular Sieve 5A column and a thermal conductivity detector. A 6890N GC (Agilent Co., USA) equipped with a Plot Q-19095P-Q04 column and a flame ionization detector was used for hydrocarbon detection. The liquid phase products were sampled and analyzed using a high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, 1260 Infinity, HPX-87H, Agilent Co., USA) with a UV detector. The Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of the main products were calculated from the total charge obtained by the potentiostat. Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) analysis of the two electrodes after catalysis was performed with the potentiostat from+ 0.5 V to – 1.3 V at a scan rate of 2 mV$s–1.

sections.heading: 3 Results and discussion
sections.text:
3.1 Characteristics of the Cu oxide nanomaterials
Figure 1 shows the SEM images and XPS spectra for the as-prepared Cu oxide NWs and NNs. The Cu oxide NWs with micrometer length were formed in the galvanostatic oxidation (Fig. 1(a)), while the potentiostatic oxidation resulted in shorter Cu oxide NNs crowded on the substrate (Fig. 1(d)). The XPS spectra of the samples (Figs. 1(b) and 1(e)) were referenced to C 1s peak at 284.69 eV. The detailed XPS spectra of Cu 2p showed two strongest peaks at 934.2 eV and 954.0 eV for the two samples, which belonged to CuO Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, respectively. The two satellite peaks located at 941.9 eVand 962.2 eV further confirmed the existence of CuO. On the other hand, the poor symmetry of the two strongest peaks suggests the existence of Cu in other valences. The AES spectra (Figs. 1 (c) and 1(f)) showed the peaks at 917 eV and 917.25 eV, respectively, both of which indicate the existence of Cu (I) in the samples. Therefore, both Cu oxide NWs and NNs contained CuO and Cu2O. On the basis of the above results and previous studies on Cu oxide synthesis via electrochemical anodic oxidation in concentrated NaCl alkaline solutions, we proposed the formation mechanisms of the Cu oxide NWs and NNs in our system.

In the Cu oxide synthesis, Cu2O could be formed spontaneously on the Cu foil substrate surface, due to the dissolved O2 in the electrolyte. Simultaneously, Reaction 4 proceeded as the corresponding cathodic reaction. When a constant potential or current was applied, CuCl1 – nn was formed (Reaction 1), and the CuCl1 – nn ion underwent chemical precipitation (Reactions 2 and 3) to form CuO, leading to a gradual decrease in the surface conductivity. In the mode of galvanostatic oxidation, the constant current kept the electrochemical driving force at the same level despite of the change in surface conductivity, forming long NWs with uniform width. In contrast, the electrochemical oxidation rate in the mode of potentiostatic oxidation
decreased along with the formation of Cu oxide, resulting in shorter NNs with an increasing width from the tip to the end. Thus, tunable surface morphologies of Cu oxide could be synthesized by simply controlling the electrochemical parameters without dose of any surfactants.
3.2 Electrochemical CO2 reduction
After electrochemical reduction of Cu oxide nanomaterials, the formed Cu NWs and NNs were examined in the electrochemical CO2 reduction. It should be mentioned that the morphologies of both Cu NWs and NNs were intact during the electrochemical reduction according to literature [23,25] and our previous study. Figures 2(a) and 2(b) shows the FEs of the main reduction products vs applied potentials. For the NWs, C2H4 gained an increasing FE from 3.1% at – 0.9 V to 12.0% at – 1.3 V, while CH4 was not detected before the potential reached – 1.2 V. Meanwhile, the FEs of CH4 were much lower than those of C2H4. In comparison, for the NNs, CH4 was observed at – 1.0 V, and gradually increased to the maximum FE of 14.3% at – 1.2 V. The FEs for C2H4 on NNs, however, were lower than those for CH4 and did not change substantially within the potential window. These results show the distinct catalytic selectivities for hydro-

carbon formation on the NWs and NNs. The NWs preferred C2H4 formation, while the NNs produced more CH4 compared to C2H4. HCOOH, the only detected liquid product in our system, exhibited a volcano-like plot of FE on the NWs with its maximum value of 24.4% at – 1.1 V. In the case of NNs, the FEs for HCOOH kept decreasing from 47.3% to 13.9% as the applied potential was changed from – 0.9 V to – 1.3 V (Fig. 2(b)). According to previous studies [11,26,27], although the detailed mechanisms of electrochemical CO2 reduction have not been fully elucidated, it is widely recognized that adsorbed CO is initially formed on the catalyst surface, followed by hydrogenation into hydrocarbons. However, due to the high kinetic barriers, the formation of CH4 or C2H4 requires a high overpotential. Thus, the FEs of CH4 and C2H4 on both NWs and NNs increase as the applied potential is shifted negatively. This result is also consistent with previous reports [23,28]. Besides, as a competing reaction in aqueous CO2 reduction, a higher applied potential would result in a faster HER, leading to the dominated H2 production. In our system, however, the FE of H2 on the Cu NWs was kept around 32% throughout the potential window. Even a lower H2 FE (ca. 17%) was achieved on the Cu NNs at the potentials negative than – 1.1 V (Fig. 2(b)). These results indicate the high electrocatalytic activity of the prepared Cu nanomaterials for CO2 reduction, and imply that the Cu NNs had a greater activity than the NWs in high overpotential regions, which could be further confirmed by the following comparisons of the current densities and LSV results. The total geometric current density (jtot) was plotted as a function of the applied potential, which was divided into two regions based on the performance. As shown in Fig. 2(c), the NWs and NNs gained a similar level of jtot in Region I, indicating their similar activities. When the applied potential was negative than – 1.1 V, the jtot of the NNs was significantly higher than that of the NWs (Region II), suggesting that the NNs had a higher activity than the NWs in this region. In addition, LSV tests of the two electrodes after CO2

reduction were also measured in 0.1 mol$L–1 KHCO3 saturated with CO2, and the results are plotted in Fig. 2(d). The obtained curves were almost the same until the potential was negative than – 1.0 V, where the NNs started to exhibit a larger current density than the NWs. This result further demonstrates that a higher electrocatalytic activity for CO2 reduction at a more negative potential was achieved on the Cu NNs. As mentioned above, the Cu NWs and Cu NNs exhibited distinct catalytic selectivities for hydrocarbon formation. The NWs produced more C2H4 than CH4, while the NNs behaved oppositely. Besides, the onset potential of CH4 on the NNs was – 1.0 V, much lower than that on the NWs, indicating a lower kinetic barrier for the CH4 formation. To compare the CH4/C2H4 selectivity, the ratios of CH4 and C2H4 on the two catalysts are presented in Fig. 3, assuming that the FEs for CH4 and C2H4 are 100% at each potential. As shown in Fig. 3(a), the Cu NWs produced C2H4 only when the potential was less negative than – 1.2 V. After that, CH4 merged and the FE ratio of C2H4 was about 70%. In the case of the Cu NNs, the FE ratio of CH4 increased from 58% at – 1.0 V to higher than 70% at – 1.3 V. Such a catalytic selectivity could be associated with the morphologies of the Cu nanomaterials. It has been reported that the surface structure of Cu, more specifically, the crystal orientation of Cu, plays a vital role in the electrochemical CO2 reduction [14,15,17,20]. The reaction mechanisms, in terms of activated barriers and intermediates, are affected by surface structure. Thus, the difference in the morphologies of the Cu NWs and Cu NNs might be the main reason for the observed distinct catalytic selectivities. Numerous efforts have been devoted to try to establish a correlation between crystal orientation and reaction pathway, however, it is still controversial regarding the fundamental principles of the morphology effects. More detailed characterizations are needed to reveal the relationship between the exact surface structure and the reaction process of the catalysts.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusions
sections.text: In this work, Cu oxide nanomaterials with tunable surface morphology, NWs and NNs, were successfully synthesized by simply controlling the electrochemical parameters in the electrochemical oxidation of Cu foils, and further reduced to Cu nanomaterials. Selective CH4 formation was observed on the Cu NNs, while selective C2H4 production was achieved on the Cu NWs. This structure sensitivity implies that it is of great importance to control the morphology of catalysts for CO2 reduction. In addition, our synthetic method offers a promising approach to prepare metal nanomaterials with tunable and variable surface morphologies.
